name: Kailasanathar Temple, Senthapoomangalam
deity: Shiva as Kailasanathar, with the Goddess Soundara Nayaki
period: Ninth and last of the Nava Kailasam, the shrine of Venus; a Pandya-era temple near the mouth of the Tamiraparani
summary: Near Athur, where the Tamiraparani ends its journey at the sea, Shiva as Kailasanathar keeps the ninth and last of the Nava Kailasam at Senthapoomangalam — the shrine of Sukran, the planet Venus.

sections.history: Senthapoomangalam, also written Serndhapoomangalam, is a village about two kilometres east of Athur on the Thoothukudi–Tiruchendur road, close to the point where the Tamiraparani, having risen in the Pothigai hills, meets the sea at Punnakayal. Its Kailasanathar temple closes the Nava Kailasam as the ninth shrine and the seat of Sukran, the planet Venus. Who built it is not certain. The temple has separate shrines for Chokkanathar and Meenakshi, the deities of Madurai, which has led to the suggestion that it was raised by a Madurai Pandya — a Kulasekhara Pandya, or Maravarman Sundara Pandya I in the thirteenth century.
sections.architecture: The temple is entered by two gateways rather than one, an unusual plan for a village shrine. Within are the sanctum of Kailasanathar and the shrine of the Goddess Soundara Nayaki, along with the Madurai pair of Chokkanathar and Meenakshi in their own shrines. A Navagraha mandapam honours the nine planets, Sukran foremost among them here. The temple tank is the Thamira Pushkarani, and the vilvam, the bael tree sacred to Shiva, is the sthala vriksham.
sections.legends: In the Nava Kailasam story, Romasa, the disciple of Agastya, set nine lotuses afloat on the Tamiraparani, and the ninth and last drifted almost to the sea before it came to rest here, completing the chain of nine shrines. The village's name is popularly read as a memory of that moment — serndha poo, "where the flower arrived". As the shrine of Sukran, the planet of beauty, comfort and harmony in marriage, it is visited by those seeking relief from an afflicted Venus in their horoscopes.
sections.festivals: Devotees offer white cloth and white lotuses to Sukran in the Navagraha mandapam, especially on Fridays, the day of Venus. Special worship is held on the new-moon days of the Tamil months of Aadi and Thai, on the monthly pradosham and on Maha Shivaratri. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Reaching Senthapoomangalam means reaching the end of the river's pilgrimage: the Tamiraparani that began the circuit at Papanasam in the hills is here broad and slow, a few kilometres from the sea. Many pilgrims time their round so that this last shrine, with its offering of white lotuses, closes the journey.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions and a midday closure; Fridays are busiest. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Men are traditionally asked to remove the upper garment before the sanctum, as at many southern shrines; follow the posted rules.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Senthapoomangalam lies in Thoothukudi district about 2 km east of Athur on the Thoothukudi–Tiruchendur road, roughly 30 km south of Thoothukudi and a short drive north of Tiruchendur. Buses on that road stop at Athur. Tiruchendur and Thoothukudi have the nearest railway stations, and Thoothukudi the nearest airport.
